analytic.title: CHaRy : The C-LAB Hard Real-Time System to Support Mechatronical Design

div.p: CHaRy is a software system to support rhe synthesis of periodic controller applications, where hard real-time conditions must De guaranteed for software tasks. Due to comple.tity reasons, CHaRj decomposes the overall problem of implementing periodic controllers on parallel embedded computers to the sub-problems partitioning, timing analysis, allocation and schedulability analysis. This rigourous decomposition is relatively new f o r hard real-time software. Since CHaRy takes into account both, the embedded controller applications as well as the encompassing system, the engineering of computer based systems (ECBS) is supported.

Since all these sub-problems are still of huge complexity, CHaRy provides eficient heuristics for all these subjects. Hence CHaRy supports the mapping of controller models (implemented by C-code) to a number of tasks (partition- ing), the extraction of their computation times (timing analysis), and their assignment to a processor network (allocation), so that all hard real-time conditions are guaranteed (schedulability analysis). This paper provides an overview ofthe system, supported by many examples.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Computer based systems (CBS) are represented by complex applications (like aircrafts, or automobiles) consisting of two main parts: the encompassing system, and a number of embedded sub-systems. In an embedded system a special purpose computer is used for the control of physical processes. Unlike in general purpose computers, realtime constraints (deadlines) on individual tasks have to be fulfilled in order to ensure correctness and safety. In such a real-time system failure can occur in the time domain as well as in the value domain, i.e. the correctness not only depends on the functional behaviour, but also on the deadlines of the results. In safety-critical systems the consequence of failure is catastrophic: It could result in death, injury, loss of property, or environmental damage. Safety-critical real-0-8186-7889-5197 $10.00 0 1997 IEEE time systems are called hard real-time systems. Examples of such systems include those that control aircrafts, automobiles, robots, and medical equipment.

Many hard real-time systems are used to control inechatronic applications, i.e. they are attached to a physical de- vice, like in a car cruise control. Most mechatronic controllers behave periodically: In an infinite loop, the current position value is read, the desired position is computed, and the new one is adjusted. The hard real-time condition is represented by a firm deadline on the computational part of the loop body. Todays computer based systems already involve many (unconnected) micro-processors in order to serve different special-purpose demands (e.g. for cruise control, anti-blocking system, motor management, etc.). However, these micro-processors are often poorly utilised, and hence many resources are wasted. If these processors were connected to each other, they would represent a parallel architecture in which the resources can be better utilised.

Hence, this paper deals with periodic controller applications, in order to run them on such a parallel embedded computer under hard real-time conditions. The new concepts presented here will help to increase utilisation (thus needing less resources, or making more complex controllers possible), and to provide free capacities for the encompassing system, like route planning in cars. Hence the needs of engineering computer based systems (ECBS) [ 131 are satisfied.

To overcome the disadvantages of hand-made controller implementations, like small complexity, unpredictability, or maintenance problems, tools have been developed to automate the design of complex controller applications (e.g. [12]). These tools are often based on relatively abstract specification or modelling levels, like differential equations (e.g. [l, 20]), Petri Nets (e.g. [19, 7]), or object-oriented real-time design methods (e.g. ROOM [21], HRT-HOOD [8]). From this high-level representation, digital controller implementations can be generated (synthesised), i.e. they are systematically transformed to a program to be run on an embedded computer.
A direct translation from the high-level representation

div.p: with regard to both structured design as well as real-time problems. This is due to the fact that high-level representations do not specify the algorithm which is used to run the controller, i.e. the way a differential equation is made discrete. Hence high-level specifications are often transformed to meta-languages (like the C programming language) to be further compiled to the executable code, which is shown in Fig. 1. Using this concept real-time problems can be handled on the basis of the meta-language.

In many cases single processor architectures are no longer suitable to cope with high computational demands of controller algorithms. In those cases controllers are implemented on parallel computers in order to speed up processing times. Hence the transformation of the meta-language to the executable code is a scheduling and allocarion problem (or multi-processor scheduling problem), as indicated by Fig. 1. Furthermore, and most important, the transformation has to take into account the hard real-time conditions. This paper provides an overview of the C-LAB Hard -Real-Time System, CHuRy. Starting from the meta-language (C-code) (see Fig. l), CHaRy automatically preassigns the corresponding periodic controller tasks to a parallel embedded computer so that the hard real-time conditions are guaranteed, and very few resources are occupied, This includes an estimation of the computation times of the tasks extracted from the meta-language. This paper particularly addresses systems in which controller algorithms are generated from high-level specifications. Due to complexity reasons CHaRy strictly decomposes the overall problem into sub-problems, which is relatively new for hard real-time software.

The paper is organised as follows: The next section illustrates how this approach is related to others. In Section 3, an overview of CHaRy is given, covering its sub-modules partitioning (Subsection 3. l), timing analysis (Subsection 3.2), allocation (Subsection 3.3), and schedulability analysis (Subsection 3.4). In Section 4 the handling of a relatively large application example is described. Finally, Section 5 gives some conclusions.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: The problem of assigning periodic controller algorithms to parallel embedded computers so that the real-time conditions are met, is very complex, even on the basis of meta-language programs. Hence a decomposition of the problem into a number of sub-problems is encouraged: 0 Partitioning is the problem of decomposing a program into a number of tasks.

0 Timing Analysis is the problem of estimating the prospective processing time of a task. Scheduling is the problem of dispatching the tasks on a single processor. Allocation (Mapping) is the problem of assigning tasks to processors, sometimes referred to as multiprocessor scheduling. In order not to get confused with the notion of scheduling, the term allocation is preferred in this paper.

0 Schedulability Analysis is the problem of verifying whether certain task assignments could cause deadline violations or not. This analysis becomes necessary whenever a heuristic is used for the scheduling problem.

Many known approaches try to handle the allocation and the scheduling problem simultaneously (e.g. [ 181). Others, like [ 171, first handle allocation and partitioning simultaneously, and then scheduling. Timing analysis can also be applied to parallel or distributed systems, as for instance the analysis of a client-server architecture presented in [23]. In that case the timing analysis has to incorporate features of schedulability analysis, i.e. the computation of the worstcase blocking time in [23]. In contrast to these approaches, the concepts of CHaRy rely on a strict decomposition of the overall problem into sub-problems, in order to handle complexity.

The rigourous problem decomposition due to complexity reasons, is very well-known in the field of hardware highlevel synthesis [ 161. However, for hard real-time software systems this is relatively new, and hence it is often not verywell supported by tools. In particular, partitioning and allocation are still often hand-made, e.g. when using HRT-HOOD or ROOM. Although problem decomposition usually leads to sub-optimal solutions, it is often the only way to handle very large systems, in contrast to methods dealing with two or more sub-problems all at once. The most popular real-time programming language is Ada. Ada is basically for hand-made designs, but it could be used as the meta-language after the partitioning process, as well. However, since the meta-language is only for internal use, almost any other programming language can be used there. as well.

div.head: CHaRy: The C-LAB Hard Real-Time System
div.p: An overview of the modules of CHaRy is shown in Fig.

CHaRy is used for running periodic controller algorithms on a parallel embedded computer so that the realtime conditions are met. CHaRy decomposes thc overall problem into the sub-problems partitioning, timing analysis, and allocation in connection with schedulability analysis. All these sub-problems are still of huge complexity. Based on efficient heuristics CHaRy provides appropriate solutions for each of them.

The main input for the system is a description of the controller algorithms implemented by a C subset. The main output is an operating system configuration (see below), i.e. the resulting task assignments. As indicated by Fig. 2, there are no global feedback loops in the design flow of CHaRy, in order to keep the computational effort low.

div.head: Partitioning
div.p: (TG = task graph, CFG = control flow graph)

div.head: Figure 3. The partitioning process
div.p: The goal of the first step, the partitioning, is to decompose the input programs into a number of tasks, using a sim-ple heuristic of finding a reasonable trade-off between task granularity and communication overhead.

The partitioning process is shown in Fig. 3. The partitioning starts with the creation of an initial task graph (TG). Each vertex of the graph represents a program statement, whereas the edges represent the dependencies between the statements. Furthermore, each vertex (statement) depicts a prospective task, and each edge depicts a prospective communication, needed to submit variable values to the destination statement. Hence the vertices are labelled with the average computational costs of the corresponding statement, and the edges are labelled with the corresponding communication overhead. The initial task graph guarantees maximum parallelism, but suffers from large communication overhead due to small task granularities.

div.head: Figure 4. An example code segment
div.p: The initial task graph (or dependency graph) of the example code segment of Fig. 4 is shown in Fig. 5. Each tasks is named after its corresponding left-hand-side variable of the assignment.

Each task graph corresponds to a certain response time, imposed by the length of the longest path in the graph, i.e. incorporating the labels at the vertices and edges. The goal of the optimisation during the iterative partitioning process is to minimise the response time, and hence reducing the size of the graph (see Fig. 3). The optimisation is done by a C-Subset 9 a Executable 4 non-guided search technique (Simulated Annealing) which slightly modifies the graph by joining a vertex with all its predecessors, or with all its successors. Then it trades the response time of the new graph against the old value. Each union of vertices is a loss of parallelism, but it reduces communication overhead by enlarging task granularities. The finial task graph of the example of Fig. 5 is shown in Fig. 6. All marked vertices are merged to "task 39", all non-marked left-hand-side vertices are merged to "task 93", and all non-marked right-hand-side vertices are merged to "task 124".

At the end of the optimisation each vertex (task) represents a number of program statements, i.e. the partitioning process is finished. Each created task is now ready for the timing-analysis process. The interface is the control flow graph (CFG) of each task (see Fig. 3). The timing analysis (see Fig. 7) is started after the partitioning process. The goal of the timing analysis is to find an estimate on the worst-case execution time (WCET) of a task (e.g. [lo]). This value is needed for later processing steps as task graph labels, in order to guarantee the hard realtime conditions. Note, that theses values are distinct from the task graph labels used during the partitioning process, where average (not maximum) values are needed. The timing analysis mainly consists of two sub-modules: caching and pipelining analysis, and longest-executablepath search (see Fig. 7). The former one incorporates the effects of caching and pipelining into the timing analysis [22]. The latter one is a heuristic to extract the longest executable path from the control flow of a given task [4]. In addition, the compilation to the executable code is part of the timing analysis.

div.head: Timing Analysis
div.p: The timing analysis is based on the control flow graph (CFG) of each task. The CFG of "task 39", created during the partitioning process (see Fig. 4, Fig. 5, and Fig. 6), is shown in Fig. 8. Each vertex represents either a block of basic statements, a branching condition, a loop, or a function. Each vertex is annotated by an attribute giving the total maximum computational effort, necessary to run the statements inside. This value is delivered by the caching and pipelining analysis (see below).
Without considering caching and pipelining strategies the WCET is often highly overestimated. The longest-

Figure 8. The corresponding CFG of task 39 of Fig. 6 including its longest executable path executable-path search is based on the knowledge of the costs for the basic blocks including the effects of caching and pipelining [22]. The caching and pipelining analysis takes place on the level of the executable code (assembler).
The resulting WCETs of the basic blocks are attached to the vertices of the control flow graph needed for the longestexecutable-path search (see Fig. 7).

Furthermore, CHaRy takes advantage of a new method that allows a combination of caching and pipelining analysis and preemption based scheduling [9], which has been limited before to either one of them. The problem that preemption-caused interrupts reset caches and pipelines had to be overcome. However, this can simply be handled by adding the overhead for refilling caches and pipelines into the schedulability analysis.

The longest-executable-path search is addressed by a new heuristic of finding an estimate on the WCET of a task [4]. It overcomes the problems of a purely structureoriented timing analysis, which analyses the control flow of the program without taking into account functional dependencies, and hence tends to overestimate the execution time. For instance, this problem is present in "task 39" (Fig. 8):

A purely structure-oriented analysis would report the length of longest structural path in the CFG as the WCET. This is a path running through all if-bodies. However, since the first and the second if-body are mutually exclusive, the purely structure-oriented analysis overestimates the WCET. The true value is given by the length of the longest executable path which is marked fold-face in Fig. 8. In general, an exact solution of this problem is impossible for larger applications due to complexity limitations. The new method used in CHaRy provides a reasonable trade-off between analysis results and analysis efforts: the results will still be better than purely structure-oriented methods without spending too much time on finding an exact solution. The actual algorithm combines path search with the concept of symbolic execution. Symbolic execution is a sort of simulated execution of the the statements on the path of interest. It will not try to evaluate each statement perfectly, and hence only try its best, i.e. without knowledge about the input values.
(TG = task graph)

div.head: Figure 9. The allocation process
div.p: The core of CHaRy is the automatic, static allocation of communicating, periodic hard real-time tasks to a point-topoint network of identical processors, so that the real-time constraints are met [ 3 ] . The allocation process is shown in Fig. 9. The tasks to be handled by the allocation are described by a number of independent task graphs, e.g. the graph of Fig. 6 or the more complex one of Fig. 10. Apart from the actual assignment of tasks to processors so that the hard real-time conditions can be guaranteed, the method tries to minimise an objective function which represents system load. This way the resources are well utilised, resulting either in cheaper solutions, or in more complex controller applications. The allocation problem is known to be NP-hard. Hence, CHaRy uses a new constructive allocation heuristic (named the Slack Method (see Fig. 9)) which is superior to listprocessing-based approaches (e.g. [ 181) with regard to both: finding more feasible solutions as well as finding solutions with better objective function values. Furthermorc, CHaRy exploits that a combination of non-guided-search (e.g. Simuluted Annealing) and constructive approaches gives better results than either of them alone. Hence the Slack Method is especially tailored to serve as a preprocessing step for a non-guided search (see Fig. 9).

Another complexity problem arises in multi-period systems with the size of the least common multiples of the period lengths (LCM). For the relatively small example of Fig. 10 with period 1 = 20 and period 2 = 14 the LCM is 140, and the number of tasks inside the LCM is 89. For larger examples the value may grow to huge numbers. Hence the Slack Method provides a new concept of dealing with multi-period systems without considering the whole LCM, by handling all transactions (= set of tasks with the same period) separately. However, the post-optimisation runs on the basis of all transactions (see Fig. 9), but does not explicitly need to inquire the whole LCM.

Due to the use of non-guided search the post-optimisation is iterative, resulting in new task assignments within each iteration step (see Fig. 9). These assignments explicitly have to be checked to verify whether the real-time conditions hold or not, using schedulability analysis (see Subsection 3.4). For scheduling a fixed-priority preemptive policy, deadline monotonic scheduling (DMS) 11 SI, is used.

The resulting task assignments represent a configuration (see Fig. 9) for the parallel real-time operating system DReaMS [ 1 I]. At run-time the operating system has only to supervise the results of this pre-analysis. Besides the guaranty of hard real-time conditions, the goal of the configuration is to reduce operating system overhead as much as possible. During the allocation process, each proccssor is assigned to be either schedule driven (SD), or OS driven (OD). SD processors are supervised by a run-time system using a batch scheduler to run fixed schedules (sometimes referred to as cyclic executives), which reduces the overhead for SD processors to almost zero. OD processors are ordinary OS-driven resources which use non-occupied capacitics to serve for other purposes (e.g. sporadic tasks, nonreal-time tasks). SD processors have only few overhead, but they are inflexible, whereas OD processors are flexible, but overhead-prone. Following this approach the advantages of both processor types are combined.

A complex example for the allocation process is given in Section 4. The schedulability analysis provided by CHaRy [2] is based on deadline-monotonic scheduling (DMS) [IS] used for dispatching the tasks on each processor. DMS is a static priority preemptive scheduling heuristic, which is an efficient way of constructing and analysing schedules for hard real-time systems. Such scheduling heuristics dispatch tasks in priority order, and the priorities remain static during run-time. Lower priority tasks can be suspended by higher priority tasks. Following the DMS policy the task deadlines are allowed to be before the end of the periods, and each task is assigned a unique priority with regard to its deadline (the smaller the deadline, the higher the priority). DMS is very well-suited for parallel environments with communicating tasks, since the effort following a sending task can be taken into consideration by reducing its deadline, and hence increasing its priority. The test on schedulability is needed during the allocation process to verify whether the hard real-time conditions are met or not (see Subsection 3.3 and Fig. 9). In such a test the ww-st-case response rime (not to be confused with the worst-case execution time of the timing analysis in Subsection 3.2) of each task is determined. This is the longest time ever taken by the task from the beginning of its period until it completes its required computation, i.e. including all possible interferences by higher priority tasks. If the worstcase response times of all tasks are less or equal to their corresponding deadlines, all hard real-time conditions are guaranteed to be met. The worst-case response times of the tasks of Fig. IO are given in Fig. 11. Due to a better runtime complexity schedulability tests (e.g. [5]) are preferred to simulation. In a simulation [ 141 the least-common multiple of the task periods has to be examined, which can last a very long time (see Subsection 3.3).

To the author's knowledge the schedulability analysis used by CHaRy is the first for event-driven parallel communicating tasks, where a task is invoked whenever its input data is completely received. All existing tests focussed on tasks with fixed release times (time-driven systems). The main disadvantage of time-driven systems is that they create a lot of additional overhead if they are used in connection with an operating system. Then one timer is needed for each tusk. However, when using an event-drivcn system, only one timer is needed for each task withoirrpredecessor.

The new and efficient test is (as many others) notnecessur), and sufficient, i.e. it does not determine an exact result (to reduce run time) but it is still guaranteed that if the task set passes the test, no deadline will be violated.

div.head: Example
div.p: CHaRy has been used to run a very complex controller application which is represented by the data in Tab. 1. The application consists of three different sub-models. The partitioning process reduced the size of the initial task graph from 7496 to 298. All tasks were handled by the timinganalysis process, in order to prepare the final allocation.

During the allocation process the communicating tasks were assigned to a given 4x3-grid network of identical processors. Due to three different sub-models, the Slack Method had to deal with three different transactions. The allocation result is shown in Fig. 12, where each square represents one processor. In the example of Fig. 12 there are only four OD processors, although there are more not very well utilised processors. On these processors it is likely that the real-time conditions could not be met, if they were converted to OD due to too much OS overhead.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The goal of this paper was to introduce CHaRy, a new system to support the synthesis of periodic controller applications, where hard real-time conditions must be guaranteed for software tasks. Due to complexity reasons, CHaRy decomposes the overall problem of implementing periodic controllers on parallel embedded computers to the sub-problems partitioning (mapping of controller models (C-code) to a number of tasks), timing analysis (extracting the computation times of a task with regard to both: caching and pipelining analysis as well as longest-feasiblepath search), allocafion (assigning the tasks to the processor network), and schedulability analysis (verifying whether all hard real-time conditions are guaranteed to be met or not).

Since all these sub-problems are still of huge complexity, CHaRy provides efficient heuristics for all these subjects. Due to the modular structure of the concept presented here, it is also possible to use the new techniques in applications beyond the scope of this paper.

CHaRy supports ECBS by taking into account both, the embedded controllcr applications as well as the encompassing system. CHaRy is part of the mechatronic project "METRO" granted by the German Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF). Within this project CHaRy is especially used to support hardware-in-the-loop simulations [ 6 ] .
